doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: The role of acoustic rhythm guitar
summary: Rhythm guitar in Basie and Eddie Condon bands, and how Marty Grosz and Rebecca Kilgore let strings ring.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: That acoustic guitar makes a big difference too.
It’s such a — we almost forget how tied that was to the Basie thing.

Yes. And not just Basie. Eddie Condon. People forget what a good guitar player he was. Not a soloist, but the time was as perfect as it could get. And it’s a lost art now, it really is, except at functions like this. Big bands don’t use rhythm guitar anymore.
Yeah. It seems to be something about the acoustic thing too.
It’s almost like you’re not hearing the chord as much as you are the — almost the washboard effect.

It depends on who’s playing it. Some players mute the strings, some let them ring. With Marty Grosz you hear the ring of the strings, which is nice. Like that’s the way Eddie Condon played. And with Rebecca Kilgore, she lets the strings ring. And it’s just a nice blend, especially with an acoustic bass. If there’s not lots of micing, that guitar, you can key everything on the rhythm guitar. You sure don’t want to be fighting that if it’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
playing all four beats. Easier for me to back off a little bit than for the guitar, so you don’t have that. And those two are two of the easiest to work with I can think of.
